title: Can, want, go, carry
goal: Use the five most common irregular verbs, combine them with the infinitive of another verb, and recognize the infinitive used as a noun.
bekal: conjugate *possum*, *volo*, *nolo*, *eo*, and *fero* in all six forms
build sentences on the pattern "want/must/can + infinitive"
read Latin proverbs with an infinitive as the subject

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Iter ad villam
dialogs.intro: Quintus is planning a trip to the family farmhouse. Not everyone is allowed to come.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Cras ad villam ire volo. Quis venire vult?
lines.id: Tomorrow I want to go to the farmhouse. Who wants to come?
lines.literal: tomorrow to house-obj go want-I. who come want-he?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Ego venire volo! Sed non possum — magister me exspectat.
lines.id: I want to come! But I can't — my teacher is expecting me.
lines.literal: I come want-I! but not can-I — teacher me-obj wait-for-he.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Ego ire possum! Nihil facere debeo.
lines.id: I can go! I don't have to do anything.
lines.literal: I go can-I! nothing-obj do must-I.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Iulia, tu domi manere debes. Litteras scribere debes.
lines.id: Iulia, you must stay home. You have to write letters.
lines.literal: Iulia, you at-home stay must-you. letter-pl-obj write must-you.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: I don't want to write letters! I want to go for a walk!

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Scribere non vis, sed dona accipere vis.
lines.id: You don't want to write, but you do want to get presents.
lines.literal: write not want-you, but gift-pl-obj receive want-you.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Pater, quid ad villam ferre debemus?
lines.id: Father, what do we have to take to the farmhouse?
lines.literal: father-call, what-obj to house-obj carry must-we?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Cibum et aquam ferre debemus. Cetera servi ferunt.
lines.id: We must take food and water. The servants carry the rest.
lines.literal: food-obj and water-obj carry must-we. rest-pl-obj servant-pl carry-they.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Possumus. Sed tu equum regere non potes!
lines.id: We can. But you can't handle a horse!
lines.literal: can-we. but you horse-obj control not can-you!

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: I can! I want to learn.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Bene dicis, filia. Qui vult, potest.
lines.id: Well said, my girl. Where there's a will, there's a way.
lines.literal: well say-you, daughter-call. who want-he, can-he.

notes: **Volo, vis, vult — three forms that look nothing alike.** The verb "want" is one of the oldest and most worn-down in Latin. Learn its sound as three separate words: *volo* (I want), *vis* (you want), *vult* (he wants). The plural is friendlier: *volumus, vultis, volunt*.

**Nolo is non + volo fused together.** *Non volo* was shortened to *nolo*, and all its forms follow: *nolo, non vis, non vult, nolumus, non vultis, nolunt*. This word gives the "don't!" command you learn in Unit 16: *noli!*

**Ire, venire, scribere, facere — the infinitive after the first verb.** When two verbs meet in one sentence, the second takes the infinitive, the dictionary form ending in *-re*. The pattern is just like English: "I want **to go**", "you must **write**".

**Qui vult, potest — a proverb worth memorizing.** Literally "the one who wants, can". Here *qui* means "the one who", and how it works is explained fully in Unit 15. For now, just learn the whole sentence; it is one of the most quoted Latin proverbs.

blocks.text: *Possum*, *volo*, *nolo*, and *malo* almost always appear with the infinitive of another verb. All four are irregular, but the last three are close siblings: learn *volo*, and the other two follow by themselves.
*Possum* is really *potis* ("able") plus *sum*, and it shows: *pot-* meets *sum* to give *possum*, meets *es* to give *potes*. If you know *sum*, you already half know *possum*.

sections.title: Eo and fero: the two wildest

blocks.text: *Eo* ("go") is so short it almost disappears; *fero* ("carry") drops its linking letter in a few places. Both are extremely common, so there's no avoiding them.

The infinitives are *ire* and *ferre*. Note *fers* and *fert*, which lose their *i*; the rest follow ordinary group three. The perfect *tuli* looks nothing like *fero* — it comes from another, older verb that gradually got attached.

*Confero* gives the abbreviation *cf.* you see in footnotes, and *refero* gives *reference*. Every compound uses exactly the same table as its parent — so once you know *eo* and *fero*, you know twenty words at once.
A Latin infinitive can stand alone as the subject of a sentence, just like "to err is human" in English. When it is the subject, any adjective describing it takes the neuter ending.

blocks.title: Patterns you can use right away
items: *… volo* — "I want to …". Example: *Latine legere volo.* — "I want to read in Latin."
*… debeo* — "I must …". Example: *Cotidie discere debeo.* — "I must study every day."
*… possum* — "I can …". Example: *Iam pauca dicere possum.* — "I can already say a few things."
*… nolo* — "I don't want to …". Example: *Nolo tacere.* — "I don't want to keep quiet."
These four patterns are enough to express almost every everyday plan and wish.
